## 1 Introduction

The endoplasmic reticulum (ER) is a membrane-bound compartment that is continuous with the nuclear envelope and extends throughout the cytoplasm of eukaryotic cells. It is the site of synthesis of most secreted proteins and of many proteins that reside in the membrane or lumen of the ER. The ER also functions as a calcium store and as the site of lipid biosynthesis. The ER is a highly dynamic organelle that is constantly remodelling in response to changes in the needs of the cell. For example, the ER expands during the secretory phase of the cell cycle and during pregnancy, when the yolk sac synthesises large quantities of yolk proteins. In contrast, the ER is reduced in size during starvation, when the cell conserves energy by reducing the synthesis of secreted proteins.

The ER is also the site of the unfolded protein response (UPR), a stress response that is activated when the ER is unable to cope with the load of unfolded proteins. The UPR is characterised by the activation of three ER transmembrane proteins: IRE1, PERK and ATF6. These proteins are normally held in an inactive state by the binding of the chaperone BiP (binding protein, also known as GRP78). When the ER is overloaded with unfolded proteins, BiP is sequestered by them, and the three proteins are released to initiate the UPR. The UPR has three main components: (i) a reduction in the rate of protein synthesis, (ii) an increase in the expression of chaperones and (iii) an increase in the expression of enzymes that degrade unfolded proteins.

The UPR is a highly conserved response that is found in all eukaryotes. It is activated by a variety of stresses, including the accumulation of unfolded proteins, the depletion of calcium and the disruption of the ER membrane. The UPR is a powerful regulator of cell fate, and its activation can lead to cell death or survival, depending on the severity of the stress and the duration of the response.
